questions.prompt: What is the difference between a value's Type and its Kind?

options.text: Type is the specific named type; Kind is the underlying category
Kind is the exact type; Type is the category

questions.explanation: Type is e.g. main.Celsius or []int; Kind is the broad category like Float64 or Slice. You switch on Kind to handle categories generically.

questions.prompt: How does encoding/json know a struct field's JSON name?

options.text: It reads the field's struct tag via reflection (field.Tag.Get("json"))
It uses the field's memory offset
It requires a separate schema file

questions.explanation: Encoders use reflection to read the json struct tag, and only see exported fields.

questions.prompt: To modify a value through reflection, what must be true, and how do you achieve it?

options.text: The Value must be settable/addressable — reflect through a pointer and use Elem()
Nothing special — any reflect.Value can be set
The value must be a string

questions.explanation: reflect.ValueOf(x) gives an unsettable copy; to mutate, use reflect.ValueOf(&x).Elem(), which is addressable and settable.

questions.prompt: Reflection is powerful but moves type errors from compile time to ____ time.
questions.explanation: A wrong reflective operation panics at runtime, so reflection sacrifices the compile-time safety of ordinary code — prefer interfaces and generics.

questions.prompt: Which are good guidelines for using reflection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Prefer interfaces and generics; use reflection as a last resort
Switch on Kind to handle type categories
Reflect through a pointer when you need to set values

questions.explanation: Reflection is slower, runtime-checked, and less readable, so reserve it for genuinely unknown types; interfaces and generics are usually better.

questions.prompt: Match each reflect concept to its meaning.

pairs.right: Get the runtime value to inspect
Read a struct field's json tag
Dereference a pointer Value to a settable one

questions.explanation: TypeOf/ValueOf are the entry points, Tag.Get reads tags, and Elem() reaches the settable value behind a pointer.
